question: A fault transmissibility index is nearly zero. What does that imply for across-fault flow, and how would a very high value change the interpretation?

result.topic: A fault transmissibility index is nearly zero. What does that imply for across-fault flow, and how would a very high value change the interpretation?
result.goal: A fault transmissibility index is nearly zero. What does that imply for across-fault flow, and how would a very high value change the interpretation?
result.final_answer:
A fault transmissibility index being nearly zero indicates minimal fluid flow across the fault plane, suggesting that the fault acts as an effective barrier to fluid movement. [KB3]
A very high fault transmissibility index implies significant fluid flow across the fault plane, indicating that the fault may act as a conduit for fluid migration rather than a barrier. [KB3]

It is very difficult to obtain an idea of the nature of the altered zone in the vicinity 
of a fault plane.  The main source of evidence is the examination of outcrops which 
exhibit faulting.  More recently core material, taken when a deviated well crosses 
a fault, has been analysed.  The main conclusion of such studies is that there exists 
two main mechanisms of alteration and these are illustrated in Figure 43.  The first 
is termed clay smearing and corresponds to ductile clay minerals from shale streaks 
being dispersed or plastered along the fault plane during tectonic movement.  The 
extent of this phenomenon is related to the frequency and thickness of shale layers in 
the original formation.  Obviously a partial displacement of a thick clean sand will 
not exhibit permeability impairment along the fault plane  because of this effect.  The 
second mechanism which has been identified is a process of localised cementation 
in the fault region e.g. precipitation of calcite or silica.

In a practical upscaling application, much attention is paid to upgridding the model
– i.e. deciding how to amalgamate the layers, so that upscaling is as accurate as pos-
sible.  The coarse grid may also be non-uniform in the x- and y-directions.
Several methods for performing non-uniform upscaling have been developed.  For 
example, Durlofsky et al. (1996, 1997) fi rst carry out a single-phase simulation.  Then
they use the inter-block fl ows to determine the coarse block boundaries. Smaller 
coarse blocks are assigned to regions where there are high fl ow rates.

using the correct boundary conditions, including wells.  We refer to this second 
method as Well Drive Upscaling (WDU).
